newsitem.title: ITALY: ALPINE SKIING-MODEST ROTEN PLAYS DOWN COMPARISONS TO SCHNEIDER.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-MODEST ROTEN PLAYS DOWN COMPARISONS TO SCHNEIDER.

text.p: Switzerland's Karin Roten played down comparisons to former queen of the slopes, compatriot Vreni Schneider, after picking up her third Alpine skiing world championship medal on Sunday.

"I don't like being compared to Vreni. She is Vreni, I am Karin," Roten said after adding a slalom bronze and giant slalom silver to the giant slalom silver she collected at last year's championships.
"We are a new generation of skiers in the Swiss team."
Roten, who -- like Schneider -- races only in the technical slalom and giant slalom disciplines, said she would be hard pressed to match Schneider's impressive record.
Schneider, who retired in 1995, won six gold medals at Olympics and world championships, as well as notching 55 World Cup victories.
"It will be almost impossible to copy Schneider. She has an incredible list of achievements," said Roten, who won her one and only World Cup medal in Lillehammer last winter.
However, the 21-year-old from Leukerbad in the German-speaking region of Switzerland, said she had learned from Schneider's mental approach to the sport.
"I was very young when Schneider celebrated the majority of her successes, so I never really got to see how she would prepare for events," Roten said.
"But I was told what she used to do for concentration and I realised I could learn a lot from it."

It was Schneider who comforted a crying Roten four years ago at a giant slalom in Soelden after the 17-year-old failed to qualify for the second run when she straddled a gate in only her second appearance on the World Cup circuit.
At the time Schneider said: "Karin has the talent to be my successor."
What still separates Roten from Schneider are gold medals.
"I am still missing a title. But I am still young and if everything continues to go well I hope to participate in many championships and Olympics," she said.

"You have to work really hard to have a great career and you also need a lot of luck. But one major injury can put a stop to the nicest dreams. Therefore, I refuse to make plans. I take things as they come."
Unlike most skiers, Roten has so far escaped serious injury. A minor knee injury forced her to take a three-week break from the slopes last summer but did not affect her training programme.
Roten was introduced to the sport at the age of three by her father, a ski instructor.
"My parents always expected a lot from us children. They pushed us very hard," said Roten, who has three brothers of whom one is also in the Swiss ski team.
In the ski-crazed Alpine nation, Roten is regarded as a role model due to her hard-work ethic. She completed business school last year despite a hectic schedule on the tour.
"I finished all my races here," she said. "I did the best I could. Now I just want to go home and celebrate."
